turns.doctor_question: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I came in because... I just, I can't stop this feeling. It's like this heavy weight all the time, and I just keep feeling like absolutely everything that goes wrong is entirely my fault. 

I mean, at work—I'm a business operations specialist, so I handle a lot of moving parts and processes, making sure things run smoothly—but lately, if even the tiniest thing gets delayed or a project hits a snag, I just spiral. I feel like I'm a completely bad employee and that I'm ruining everything for my team. And it's not just work, it's at home, too. I bought this house, which I worked so hard to save for after I got my degree, but now... I look around and if a pipe leaks or the yard gets a little overgrown, I just think about what a terrible homeowner I am. 

It's like I'm convinced I just deserve to lose everything I've worked for. I sit there and overthink every single mistake I've ever made, and I just can't shake this intense guilt that I'm failing everyone around me. I just... I don't know how to stop thinking that I deserve to be fired or lose my house. It just plays on a loop in my head, and I can't turn it off, no matter how hard I try to rationalize it.

symptom_reasoning.S030: The patient describes intense, persistent feelings of guilt, believing everything that goes wrong is their fault, and feeling worthless as an employee and homeowner.

turns.doctor_question: Have you experienced periods like this in the past, or is this the first time you have felt this way?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, it's definitely not the first time. I mean, I wish it was, because then maybe I could just brush it off as a bad week or a bad month, you know? But honestly... it's been going on for a really long time. I was actually trying to figure out exactly when it started the other day, because I was looking through some old emails from work, trying to see when I stopped caring about the quarterly reports—which I used to love doing, by the way, I used to love finding the efficiencies and fixing the bottlenecks. But I realized that this feeling, this just absolute heaviness and total loss of interest in everything I used to care about, it's been with me for about two years and one month. 

I remember because it was right around the time we were doing the end-of-year audits two years ago, and I just... I couldn't bring myself to care. And it hasn't stopped since then. Two whole years, plus a month. Every single day waking up and just feeling like there's a wet blanket over my brain. I used to go hiking on the weekends, I used to actually enjoy decorating the house I told you about, but for the last twenty-five months, give or take a few days, I just come home and stare at the wall. It's just been this endless, dragging period where nothing brings me joy anymore, and it's exhausting just trying to pretend that I'm fine when it's been going on for over two years.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes a persistent 'absolute heaviness,' feeling like there is a 'wet blanket over my brain,' and experiencing an 'endless, dragging period.'
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly reports a 'total loss of interest in everything I used to care about,' no longer caring about work or hobbies like hiking and decorating, and states that 'nothing brings me joy anymore.'

turns.doctor_question: During these past two years, have there been any specific periods where your symptoms became significantly more intense or severe, to the point where you felt much worse than your usual 'baseline' of feeling this way?
turns.patient_response:
Well, looking back... I mean, I've really been trying to analyze it, to see if there was some pattern or trigger, because as an operations specialist, that's what I do, right? I look for the root cause of an issue. But honestly, it's just been this constant, heavy baseline. The low mood, the total loss of interest in everything—like I said, the hiking, the house, the reports—it's just been there for almost the entire time since this whole thing started. 

It's not like I have these massive spikes where it suddenly gets a hundred times worse and then goes back to normal. It's more like... it's just always bad. Always heavy. There have been a few, very brief periods where maybe I could function just a little bit better, where I could actually push through a workday without feeling like I was completely failing everyone, or where I could maybe manage to do a load of laundry without staring at the washing machine for an hour. But those moments are so fleeting. They don't last. Before I know it, I'm right back down in that same trench, feeling that same constant, draining emptiness. It's just been this long, drawn-out stretch of feeling low, basically the whole two years and one month, with barely any real break from it.

turns.doctor_question: During these past two years, have there ever been any periods where you felt like yourself again—meaning your mood and interest were back to normal—that lasted for two months or longer?
turns.patient_response:
Well... no. No, definitely not for two whole months. I mean, I try to think back and map it out in my head, like putting it on a timeline, right? Because I really want to give you an accurate answer. I want to say yes, I want to tell you that there was a whole season where I was just me again, where I could wake up and make coffee and actually care about the taste of it, or go to work and feel that old satisfaction when a project closed out successfully. But... I just can't. 

If I'm being completely honest, any time I've felt even a tiny bit lighter, it's been so incredibly short-lived. Like, maybe a few days, or a week at the absolute most, where the fog lifts just enough for me to think, "Oh, maybe I'm getting better, maybe this is the turning point." I remember one time last spring, I actually went out and bought some new throw pillows for the living room, which sounds so stupid, but it felt like a huge deal at the time because I actually cared about how the couch looked. But then, by the following Tuesday, I was right back to looking at those pillows and just feeling completely numb, like they were mocking me for thinking I could actually be a normal person who enjoys decorating. 

So, no, there hasn't been any stretch of time that lasted anywhere close to two months where I felt normal. It's just been this continuous, heavy slog. The moments of feeling okay are just blips on the radar, you know? They just disappear before I can even really register that they happened, and then I'm right back to the guilt and the exhaustion. It's never been two months. Not even close.

symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient expresses an inability to feel their 'old satisfaction' or care about things they used to enjoy.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly mentions returning to a state of 'exhaustion.'

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or the amount you eat since this period of feeling low began?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that's... that's a whole other thing I've been trying to track, honestly. Because, you know, in my job, inputs and outputs are everything. If the inputs are off, the outputs are going to be a mess. And my appetite has just been completely all over the place since this whole thing started. It's like my body forgot how to regulate itself. 

Mostly, I just... I don't eat real meals anymore. Especially during the day. I used to meal prep on Sundays—I'd make these little quinoa bowls with roasted vegetables and chicken, all perfectly portioned out in Tupperware for the week. It was efficient, it was healthy. But now? The thought of chopping a vegetable just feels like climbing a mountain. So I just skip lunch entirely. I'll sit at my desk, or on the couch if I'm working from home, and I just drink coffee. So much coffee, just trying to cut through that wet blanket feeling in my brain. And then maybe I'll have a piece of toast. Just dry toast, or maybe some butter if I can manage to get it out of the fridge. 

I just gravitate toward whatever is absolute lowest effort. Whatever is easiest. And it's definitely having an effect, because I was getting dressed the other day—well, trying to get dressed in actual work pants instead of sweatpants—and I realized they were just hanging off me. My clothes are definitely looser. I haven't stepped on a scale because, frankly, I don't want another metric to obsess over and feel bad about, but I can feel it in how my clothes fit. It's just... I know I should eat better, I know I need the energy, but the drive to actually prepare and consume a full, nutritious meal is just completely gone. It's just coffee, toast, and whatever doesn't require me to actually try.

symptom_reasoning.S026: The patient reports a significant decrease in appetite, skipping meals, and noticeable weight loss evidenced by her clothes fitting more loosely.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient describes a profound lack of energy, stating that simple tasks like chopping vegetables feel like 'climbing a mountain' and she only has the drive for the 'absolute lowest effort'.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient mentions drinking excessive coffee to try and cut through a 'wet blanket feeling in my brain', indicating clouded thinking and diminished mental clarity.

turns.doctor_question: How has your sleep been during these past two years?
turns.patient_response:
Well, my sleep is... it's just as chaotic as everything else, to be honest. I've actually tried tracking it, you know, with one of those sleep apps on my phone, because I figured if I could just see the data, maybe I could optimize it. But the data is just a mess. It's incredibly frustrating because I know how crucial restorative sleep is for cognitive function, especially when I'm trying to review these complex operational flowcharts at work, but I just can't seem to get my brain to shut down. 

Most nights, I go through this whole routine—I make sure the room is cool, I turn off all the screens, I do everything you're supposed to do—and then I just lie there. I lie awake for hours. It's like my body is exhausted, completely drained, but my mind is just spinning, or sometimes not even spinning, just... stuck. I just lie there listening to the house settle. I hear the refrigerator click on, I hear the pipes creak, I hear every single tiny noise, and I just stare at the ceiling. And then, if I do finally manage to drift off, it's not even good sleep. Because without fail, I wake up around three or four in the morning. 

And once I'm awake at that hour, that's it. It's over. I'll toss and turn, I'll try flipping the pillow, I'll try counting backward from a thousand, but I just can't get back to sleep before my alarm goes off for work. It's this agonizing stretch of time where it's too late to go back to sleep but too early to actually get up and start the day. So I just lie there, feeling that heavy, dreadful feeling, knowing that I'm going to have to drag myself through another day on three hours of sleep. It's just... it's every night. It's exhausting.

symptom_reasoning.S027: The patient describes lying awake for hours (initial insomnia) and waking up at 3 or 4 AM unable to get back to sleep (early morning awakening).
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly states their body is 'exhausted, completely drained' and describes the daily experience as 'exhausting'.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any change in how you move or speak, such as feeling like you are physically slowed down or, conversely, feeling restless and unable to sit still?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely the first one. The slowing down. And it's... it's honestly so embarrassing, especially at work, because, like I said, my whole job is about efficiency and operations. I'm supposed to be the one streamlining things, making sure everything runs smoothly and quickly. But lately, I feel like I'm the bottleneck. 

It's worst in the mornings. I'll get to my desk, and just the physical act of getting started is monumental. I'll sit there, and I know I need to open my spreadsheets—I have these master trackers that I need to update first thing—but my hands just feel so heavy. It's like... it's like I'm moving through wet cement. That's the only way I can describe it. Every movement takes so much deliberate effort. Even just typing out a response to a simple email, my fingers don't want to hit the keys. I'll stare at the keyboard, and my brain is saying "type," but my hands are just lagging behind, like there's a disconnect between my brain and my muscles. 

And walking... oh my gosh, walking to a meeting. Our office has this long hallway that connects the operations department to the main conference rooms, and usually, I'd just power-walk down it, you know, grab my laptop, maybe a coffee, and just go. But now, I feel like I'm shuffling. I can feel my feet dragging. I had a meeting last week with the logistics team, and I realized I was walking so slowly that I was actually going to be late, even though I left my desk with plenty of time. I tried to speed up, I really tried to force myself to just walk normally, but it felt like I was wearing lead boots. I think people are noticing, too. My manager asked me the other day if I was feeling okay because I seemed "low energy," which is just corporate speak for "you're moving like a zombie." It's incredibly frustrating because I want to move fast, I want to be sharp, but my body just refuses to cooperate. It's just this constant, heavy resistance to everything I try to do physically.

symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient explicitly describes severe physical slowing, stating that moving feels like 'pushing through wet cement,' their hands feel heavy, and they shuffle or drag their feet when walking.
